evidence: src/invoice/invoice.service.ts: `issue(orderId: string, amount: number)` and `countFor(orderId: string)` deal with InvoiceEntity through `invoiceRepository`, which fits the invoice concern.
src/invoice/invoice.service.ts: `validateCreate(quantity: number): void { assertCreateRule(quantity); }` forwards to the order module's creation rule.
src/invoice/invoice.service.ts: `import { assertCreateRule } from '../order/order.service';` shows the rule is owned by order.service.
`issue()` never calls `validateCreate`, so the method has no link to invoice issuing and only re-exposes an order invariant.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: src/invoice/invoice.service.ts is mostly about invoices: `issue(orderId, amount)` and `countFor(orderId)` both go through the module's own `Repository<InvoiceEntity>`. The third public method, `validateCreate(quantity: number)`, is the problem. It only forwards to `assertCreateRule` from `../order/order.service`. That is an order-creation rule based on `quantity`, and invoices have no quantity field (they use `amount`). Even `issue()` never calls this check. So the invoice service's public API offers a second way to reach a rule that belongs to the order module. That mixes order validation into the invoice service and spreads one rule across two module surfaces, when callers should go to its single owner. The logic itself is delegated rather than copied, so the risk of duplication is limited. That is why confidence is moderate. Import direction is out of scope and was not part of this judgment.
